rounds.proof_sketch: The input specification fixes dtype=torch.float32, so scalar_t=float via AT_DISPATCH_FLOATING_TYPES. Variable val0 is type scalar_t=float. The original code has fabsf((float)val0) where the (float) cast on a float variable is a no-op. The mutated fabsf(val0) is semantically identical since val0 is already float. Both expressions produce identical results for all possible float32 values.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation removes an explicit (float) cast from val0 before passing it to fabsf(). Since the input tensor dtype is fixed at torch.float32, the AT_DISPATCH_FLOATING_TYPES macro instantiates the kernel with scalar_t=float. Therefore, val0 is already a float, and the cast (float)val0 is a no-op identity conversion. The mutated code fabsf(val0) produces bitwise identical results to fabsf((float)val0) because no actual type conversion occurs. This is confirmed by Layer 2 testing which found bitwise equivalence across 112 test rounds including stress tests with large magnitudes, near-zero, sparse, and boundary values.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable under fixed float32 dtype. The cast removal only matters if scalar_t were double (when input dtype is float64), but dtype is fixed as float32 in the contract.
rounds.recommendations: For mutation testing of type casts in templated CUDA kernels, the testing framework should consider generating inputs with different dtypes (float32 vs float64) if the kernel supports multiple types via AT_DISPATCH_FLOATING_TYPES. The cast (float)val0 would only be semantically meaningful when scalar_t=double, causing precision loss that the explicit cast makes intentional.
